item.title: Rule-Guided and Trajectory-Aware Repair for LLM-Based HLS Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising path for directly generating functionally correct and synthesizable HLS-C from natural-language specifications. However, existing approaches often struggle to turn multi-round tool feedback and reusable HLS knowledge into effective revisions, limiting end-to-end generation success. We propose MementoHLS, an agentic HLS generation framework built around executable and falsifiable dual-memory-guided repair. MementoHLS combines an Executable Repair Contract Library (ERCL), which converts cross-task HLS knowledge into evidence-gated repair actions, with a Reviewer-Grounded Falsification Ledger (RFL), which converts task-local repair history into trajectory evidence to suppress ineffective routes and preserve validated progress. To ensure reliable outcome attribution, a Same-Candidate Reviewer binds Parse, Compile, Testbench (TB), and Synthesis (Synth) outcomes to the corresponding candidate, while a Single-Commit Arbiter commits at most one candidate per round. Evaluated on 94 HLS-Eval and 170 Bench4HLS tasks, MementoHLS improves same-candidate TB$\wedge$Synth pass@1/pass@5 from 41.7%/57.4% to 58.9%/68.1% on HLS-Eval, and from 15.5%/32.9% to 32.4%/50.6% on Bench4HLS, demonstrating substantial improvements in end-to-end HLS generation reliability.
item.dc:creator: Xianjing Zhu, Wenqi Lou, Yuanbo Wen, Teng Wang, Lei Gong, Chao Wang, Xuehai Zhou

item.title: A Synchronized Tri-Modality Wireless System for Multi-Point Non-Contact Cardiac Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.07358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cardiac physiological monitoring is fundamental to evaluating cardiovascular health and diagnosing related diseases. Non-contact radar sensing can capture chest-wall vibrations with spatial specificity, enabling localized physiological monitoring and cardiac assessment. Progress, however, has been limited by the absence of a reliable, research-grade hardware platform for rigorous validation of radar-based methods. Prior systems typically pair radar, namely Doppler cardiography (DCG), with only electrocardiography (ECG) or other coarse references, providing no direct mechanical ground truth and thus constraining fine-grained evaluation of radar outputs. We present a tri-modality wireless system that integrates ECG, seismocardiography (SCG), and DCG under a unified acquisition and control framework for time-aligned recording and analysis. The tri-modality system combines miniaturized wearable ECG/SCG modules with a high-resolution mmWave radar module, supporting spatially resolved sensing and subsequent feature extraction. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated ECG--SCG--DCG hardware system for comprehensive cardiac monitoring; it enables multi-point thoracic acquisition, achieves precise cross-modal synchronization, and maintains specifications suitable for wearable operation. Experiments on a linear-motion platform show close agreement between DCG- and SCG-derived displacements, confirming accurate displacement measurement. Human-subject studies further demonstrate cross-modal consistency and robust extraction of feature points, establishing ECG as the electrical anchor and SCG as the mechanical ground truth for DCG. Overall, the system provides a rigorous, spatially resolved validation platform that advances non-contact cardiac sensing and supports next-generation radar-based monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Wei Ren, Kaili Zhao, Huansheng Yi, Miaoyang Hu, Jianqi Wang, Canhua Xu, Fugui Qi

item.title: OpenRDMA: A GPU-Native Multi-Path Reliable RDMA Transport Architecture
item.description: arXiv:2611.07559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the computing power density of large-scale AI clusters rises, network communication increasingly limits system performance. GPU-initiated communication requires low-overhead request submission to overlap communication with computation. However, GPUDirect RDMA (GDR) still relies on CPU involvement in its control path, while InfiniBand GPUDirect Async (IBGDA) requires GPUs to assemble Work Queue Entries (WQEs), consuming additional SM resources and memory bandwidth. We propose OpenRDMA, an open-source multi-path reliable RDMA transport architecture designed for GPU-friendly communication. First, OpenRDMA provides a minimal GPU doorbell mechanism: the GPU issues an 8-byte token, and a dedicated FPGA NIC reconstructs the complete WQE from preconfigured context. Second, building on Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC), OpenRDMA supports per-packet multi-path transport and out-of-order arrivals, while selective retransmission, ordered DMA placement, and GPU-visible flag polling provide reliable delivery and safe data consumption. Third, a hardware-software co-designed retransmission mechanism keeps the GPU submission path lightweight and reduces FPGA hardware state overhead: the NIC handles fast data transfer, while CPU software manages complex timeout detection, state tracking, and recovery policies. We describe the architecture and key hardware components of OpenRDMA; implementation of the FPGA prototype is underway.
item.dc:creator: Ziheng Ji, Chunyu Liu, Weihao Peng, Mingheng Mi, Pu Wang, Hai Zhang

item.title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2611.07707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Orhun G\"orkem, Athanasios Vasilopoulos, Georgios Pagonis, Victoria Clerico, Hadjer Benmeziane, Irem Boybat, Hsinyu Tsai, Abu Sebastian, William Andrew Simon

item.title: Should You Split Decode? Disaggregation Across Future Models and Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2611.08299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For large language model (LLM) inference, prefill/decode disaggregation (P/D) is deployed in production to isolate phases with different resource demands. Attention/feed-forward network disaggregation (AFD) splits decode again, but adds communication, placement constraints, and another provisioned pool. We ask whether role-specific placement repays this cost as models and accelerator roadmaps change. Infrastructure is committed before future models and hardware can be benchmarked. We present SiliconForge, a calibrated model that varies the serving decomposition and hardware assignment independently. We compare P/D and P/D+AFD across four model directions, four accelerator classes anchored to current and announced parts, and two fabrics. We co-optimize each design using the same rules for pipeline overlap and the same power budget. Our main comparisons show no robust deployment-level AFD advantage in service-level objective (SLO) goodput per kW. Most nominal estimates favor P/D. The largest AFD lead comes from fitting one more prefill replica, not from a more efficient decode pool. AFD has a nominal lead in the KV-heavy (key-value) model direction when the co-located expert pool spans several small scale-up domains. Larger domains or a fast fabric for both designs weaken that lead. We therefore find that prefill provisioning, decode memory bandwidth, links, and pool granularity decide deployments more than the split alone. A fixed hardware assignment can lose its advantage as models, fabrics, hardware assumptions, and objectives change. Re-optimizing mappings and pool sizes on the same hardware cuts early commitment's median normalized goodput loss from 36% to 9%. We recommend adjustable mappings and pool sizes to let boundary and hardware choices follow model demands.
item.dc:creator: Ramyad Hadidi

item.title: Scaling Up Analog CIM: A Simulation Framework for Topology-Aware Mapping
item.description: arXiv:2611.08399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient AI inference by performing in-situ matrix multiplication. The growing demand for deploying larger models motivates chiplet integration to expand CIM capacity. However, simulation abstractions based on local operator costs and aggregate communication metrics obscure the impact of weight-mapping topology when CIM system scales up. We develop a phase analysis that quantifies how strongly mapping topology affects system performance across hardware configurations and how mapping optimization translates into latency gains. To evaluate and exploit this design space, we present Isobar, a simulation platform integrating CIM decompositions, heterogeneous execution, and resource modeling. Validated against silicon measurements and cycle-accurate simulation, Isobar provides reliable cost estimates that enable effective mapping search across model and hardware configurations. For Gemma-7B prefill, Isobar-guided mapping reduces communication time by 23.3% and end-to-end latency by 18.6% relative to the strongest baseline. Isobar's system-level modeling show that analog CIM retains energy-efficiency potential relative to GPU when scaled to thousands of dies, and identify topology-aware mapping as a key design dimension for efficient execution.
item.dc:creator: Yuxin Ren, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang

item.title: Energy Measurement and Optimization of TinyML in Resource-Constrained Embedded Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.07264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the volume of data generated at the network edge, where many devices operate under severe memory, processing, and energy constraints. In this context, Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables machine learning (ML) tasks to be executed on microcontrollers, smart sensors, and other resource-constrained platforms. However, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding the algorithms evaluated, energy-measurement methods, reported metrics, influencing factors, and optimization strategies. This study presents a systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research. It identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines the technical factors affecting energy consumption, and organizes the reported optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. The findings highlight the frequent use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, direct measurements and analytical estimations, and factors related to model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision, and input characteristics. The optimization strategies were grouped into model compression, hardware-aware design, system and communication optimization, and data and processing optimization. The results also reveal limited standardization in experimental platforms, measurement procedures, and reporting practices, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison across studies. This mapping provides an updated overview of the field and guidance for developing and evaluating more energy-efficient TinyML solutions.
item.dc:creator: Clariele Almeida, Renan Beserra, Rafael Moura, Danilo Ara\'ujo, Bruno Nogueira, S\'ergio Chevtchenko, Ermeson Andrade

item.title: Memory Fit: Architectural Support for Page Placement by Learning Models of Good Behavior
item.description: arXiv:2611.07506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Server main memory is increasingly heterogeneous, incorporating technologies such as zswap, CXL memory expanders, and emerging phase-change memories (PCM). To decide where to place pages, operating systems have to choose between efficient but coarse-grained access bits, out-of-band profiling, or costly runtime instrumentation. This paper proposes memory fit, a hardware abstraction that provides precise and accurate page placement information to an operating system. Memory fit measures how well a page "fits" each type of memory in the system. Memory fit separates the mechanism of measuring affinity between pages and memories from the OS policy of choosing which pages to move when. The paper describes soft trace matching (STM), a computationally and space efficient algorithm to compute memory fit. The key technical insight behind STM is that it can estimate memory fit by comparing accesses to a page with a learned model of "good" traces for a memory. We have implemented memory fit and STM in a BOOMv3 RISC-V processor running Linux 6.6. On extended GUPS, memory fit placements recover 2.2-3.8 times as much of the performance gap to optimal placement as Linux TPP. For Redis with equal DRAM and PCM capacities, placements selected by memory fit recover 80% of the performance gap, versus 19% for TPP, in a placement replay. Memory fit requires only 64 bits of state per 4 KiB page and can be updated on every main-memory access with only a 1.2% overhead of OS kernel notification processing.
item.dc:creator: Chun Deng, Hui Sub Shim, Evan Laufer, Anna Eaton, David Tennenhouse, Tsachy Weissman, Philip Levis

item.title: MCUFlowNet: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Optical Flow on Microcontrollers
item.description: arXiv:2611.08147v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.
item.dc:creator: Enmin Lin, Jona Beysens

item.title: Zirah: A Post-Quantum True Random Number Generator Hardware Signer With an Avalanche Noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.08200v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Zirah is a hardware signer built around an STM32F407 microcontroller, and its purpose is to find out, on inexpensive hardware, where a post-quantum signing key is exposed and what actually protects it. The device draws every random bit from a reverse-biased 2N3904 junction in avalanche breakdown, amplified by an LM358 and screened by SP 800-90B health tests, computes ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, hedged) on the STM32 with two-share arithmetic masking of the secret-key multiplications, and adds ECDSA P-256 from an ATECC608 secure element over the same digest, once a person has matched an eight-digit digest prefix on its OLED with the PC and pressed a button. A desktop application and a command-line tool drive the board and verify its output, and because only a 32-byte manifest digest reaches the device, it signs files of any type and size, returning signed copies for PDF, Office Open XML, ZIP, PNG and JPEG files and detached records for every other format. NIST's SP 800-90B tool rejected the IID assumption for 1,000,000 raw samples and assessed 6.898 bits of min-entropy per byte on the non-IID track, against the 1 bit the firmware credits, while spectral lines near 116 Hz that hold about 5 % of the variance remain unexplained. At 168 MHz the masked signature took a median of 157 ms over 20 runs and a complete signing operation under 0.8 s, and the signer matched the pq-crystals reference in 1,976 checks natively and on an emulated Cortex-M4. The ATECC608 can neither store the 4,032-byte ML-DSA-65 key nor compute with it, so that key sits in ordinary flash behind readout protection, and on an earlier board, before that protection was enabled, a debugger copied it out and the copy produced a valid ML-DSA-65 signature without the device, although the leakage results come from an instruction-level emulator and nothing here is certified.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Shaheer Bin Junaid

item.title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
item.description: arXiv:2611.08380v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory, and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $\mu$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.
item.dc:creator: Hamid Noori, Carlton Shepherd

item.title: Analysis of LLM Vulnerability to GPU Soft Errors: An Instruction-Level Fault Injection Study
item.description: arXiv:2601.19912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are highly compute- and memory-intensive, posing significant demands on high-performance GPUs. At the same time, advances in GPU technology driven by shrinking transistor sizes and lower operating voltages have made these devices increasingly susceptible to soft errors, particularly in radiation-prone environments such as satellite computing scenarios. While prior work has examined GPU soft errors, most studies have focused on general-purpose applications or conventional neural networks primarily used for vision tasks such as classification and detection. However, vulnerability analysis of modern LLMs remains limited, despite their rapid adoption in diverse application scenarios. Given the unique characteristics of LLMs, their resilience to soft errors may differ substantially from earlier models. To bridge this gap, we conduct the first instruction-level fault injection study of LLM inference to analyze the factors affecting LLM vulnerability. Our approach reveals reliability characteristics from multiple perspectives, highlighting the effects of model architecture, parameter scale, and task complexity. These findings provide new insights into LLM reliability and inform the design of more effective fault tolerance mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Duo Chai, Zizhen Liu, Shuhuai Wang, Songwei Pei, Cheng Liu, Huawei Li, Shangguang Wang

item.title: An Extended Study of Gear-Ratio-Aware Standard Cell Layout Generation for DTCO Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2603.13665v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Advanced nodes decouple contacted poly pitch (CPP) and lower-metal pitch to improve routability. We present CPCell, an efficient standard-cell layout generation framework, to support arbitrary gear ratio (GR) and offset parameters through a fine-grained layered grid graph and constraint-programming-based placement-routing co-optimization. Layout quality is improved via Middle-of-Line routing, M0 pin enablement, pin accessibility constraints and a weighted multi-objective formulation that jointly optimizes cell layouts. To scale to netlists with up to 48 transistors, we incorporate acceleration techniques including transistor clustering, identical transistor partitioning, routing lower bound tightening and early termination strategies. Comprehensive cell-level and block-level studies are conducted to evaluate GR and offset choices, quantify the benefits of the proposed objectives and assess their impact on power, performance, area and IR-drop outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Chung-Kuan Cheng, Andrew B. Kahng, Bill Lin, Yucheng Wang, Dooseok Yoon

item.title: Implementing Keyword Spotting on the MCXN947 Microcontroller with Integrated NPU
item.description: arXiv:2506.08911v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper presents a keyword spotting (KWS) system implemented on the NXP MCXN947 microcontroller with an integrated Neural Processing Unit (NPU), enabling real-time voice interaction on resource-constrained devices. The system combines MFCC feature extraction with a CNN classifier, optimized using Quantization Aware Training to reduce model size with minimal accuracy drop. Experimental results demonstrate a 59x speedup in inference time when leveraging the NPU compared to CPU-only execution, achieving 97.06% accuracy with a model size of 30.58 KB, demonstrating the feasibility of efficient, low-power voice interfaces on embedded platforms.
item.dc:creator: Petar Jaku\v{s}, Hrvoje D\v{z}apo

item.title: BRIDGE: Lazy-Move Compilation for Dual-Species Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
item.description: arXiv:2606.31833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neutral-atom quantum computers commonly connect distant qubits by transporting atoms, incurring trap-handover errors, heating, and atom loss. We present BRIDGE (Buffer-Relay Interconnect for Data-stable Gate Execution), a hardware--software co-design that connects stationary data atoms through a fixed, second-species buffer network. Short buffer chains mediate remote controlled-Z gates and return to their initial states after each operation. BRIDGE-F combines relay routing with buffer-mediated SWAPs to relocate quantum states without transporting atoms. BRIDGE-H additionally permits data-atom transport when its full modeled cost is offset by higher survival-weighted fidelity. Across 21 circuits, BRIDGE-F exceeds ZAP and Enola in modeled survival-weighted fidelity, with geometric-mean ratios of $2.1\times$ and $38\times$ and medians of $1.3\times$ and $3.7\times$. Modeled execution latency is lower by factors of approximately $500$ and $1{,}350$, respectively, with circuit single-qubit costs excluded and relay/SWAP Hadamards included. On the same fabric, BRIDGE-F matches or exceeds SABRE-based routing on 17 circuits. Rescoring nominal plans with relay-module error equal to direct-CZ error preserves the advantage over ZAP across all 21 circuits, although recompilation can underperform on QFT. These results identify stationary buffer-mediated connectivity as a promising alternative to repeated atom transport under the stated physical assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Chen Huang, Jingbo Wang, Zhemin Zhang, Ming Zhong, Zhuo Fu, Zhiding Liang, Yuan Sun, Dong E. Liu

item.title: TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2611.06079v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq's Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware schedulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condition for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code structure. We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The programmer schedules operations, loops, and composed kernels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring schedules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR, its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear program, using explicit times to group connected operations into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycleaccurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves a $1.40\times$ latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cycle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636 GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at 32.
item.dc:creator: Xuxiao Yang, Junchi Wu, Yuqi Peng, Feiyang Wu, Zhuoran Li, Wei Kong, Shuo Tao, Dongyi Fan, Yiming Zhang, Keqin Luo, Xingrui Gao, Xuehai Qian, Youwei Zhuo
